newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - January 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - January 23.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- HERITAGE BLOCK ON MILLENNIUM TOWER

Plans by construction and engineering group Kvaerner to build Europe's tallest building in the City of London have been thwarted after English Heritage refused planning permission for the site earmarked for the development. Kvaerner had planned to build the 92-storey, 1,265-foot Millennium Tower on the site of the former Baltic Exchange, which was severely damaged by an IRA bomb in 1992.
-- CREDIT SUISSE BREAKS RANKS BY URGING HOLOCAUST FUND

The chairman of Credit Suisse Group has called for the establishment of a "well-endowed" fund for the survivors and relatives of victims of the Holocaust who left their money in Swiss banks. The call for the fund, which would be set up as a goodwill gesture, breaks with the rest of Switzerland's banking community and demonstrates the confusion among the banks as to how to respond to claims that they helped finance Germany's war effort and are concealing dormant bank accounts of Holocaust victims.
-- LEGAL ACTION LAUNCHED OVER WORLD CUP STADIUM

Legal action has been launched against the French government by the European Commission, after claims that the award of a contract to build and run the centerpiece stadium of the 1998 World Cup tournament breached European competition rules. The case is unlikely to have an effect on the construction of the stadium, but could be referred to the European Court of Justice if France does not respond to the Commission's concerns within the next two months.
-- CLARKE MAY RESIST RATE RISE CALL AS RETAIL SALES DECLINE

Figures from Britain's Office of National Statistics have revealed a surprise marked slowdown in high street sales last month. The unexpected downturn, the biggest drop in retail sales volumes in 16 months, has prompted speculation that Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke may be able to leave interest rates unchanged until after the general election.
-- VAN MIERT KEEPS UP THE PRESSURE OVER BA DEAL

Karel van Miert, the European Union's competition commissioner, has maintained his opposition to the proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines by reiterating his threat to take the UK to court if the government approves the deal. He said that although the proceedings at the European Court could take years, the deal would meanwhile remain illegal without approval from Brussels, and that would allow rival airlines to challenge the alliance in their national courts.
-- REGULATOR WARNS RAIL GROUPS OVER TICKETING

The regulator of Britain's railway industry, John Swift, has issued a warning to the newly privatized train-operating companies to improve ticketing information to customers. He promised that anonymous researchers will make 5,200 checks over the next two months to assess the quality of information provided to customers. The move follows concern that passengers are unwittingly paying too much for tickets and not being informed about the services of rival operators.
-- GOWRIE ATTACKS CORPORATE STANDARDS

Lord Gowrie, the former government minister, has opened a debate in the House of Lords on self-regulation in British financial circles by attacking current standards of corporate governance. Lord Gowrie, who is a director of several public companies, accused large institutional shareholders of being more concerned about getting business for their allied merchant banks than about exercising proper control over company boards. Gowrie also called for more careful selection of non-executive directors, including vetting by the Securities and Investment Board.
-- GEC SPLIT INTO FIVE BY SIMPSON

George Simpson, the new managing director of General Electric Company, has restructured the electronics and engineering combine into five divisions. With the moves Simpson, who replaced Lord Weinstock in the post in September, will abolish the idiosyncratic reporting systems developed by his predecessor. The day-to-day running of the new divisions will be handed over to managing directors.
-- TELEWEST NEARS NETWORK DEAL TO LINK FRANCHISES

Cable company Telewest Communications is reported to be in advanced talks with several telecommunications groups over the creation of a telecoms network linking its cable franchises in the UK. The deal would enable Telewest, the biggest cable company in the UK, to bypass the expensive interconnection charges paid by cable companies to join British Telecom's system. Telewest is to invest 50 million stg in the Inter-Franchise Network, a venture involving BRT, the former British Rail telecoms network.
-- NTT WEIGHS UP MOVE WITH BT INTO FRENCH TELECOMS

Japanese telecoms company NTT is considering a 300 million stg investment alongside British Telecom in the French telecoms market. The move follows the announcement last month by NTT that it is seeking to move into international markets. NTT is said to be considering taking a 10 percent stake in new French telecoms operator Cegetel, the company in which British Telecom is investing 1.1 billion stg for a 25 percent stake.
